{{Short description|1869–1947 Japanese system of nobility}} {{For|the 1970 Japanese film|Kazoku (film)}} {{Italic title}}
[[File:Yōshū Chikanobu House of Peers.jpg|thumb|right|300px|The [[:en:House of Peers|House of Peers]] in session with {{ill|Emperor Meiji|en|Emperor Meiji|qid=Q174231|lt=Emperor Meiji|1=Emperor Meiji}} giving a speech. ([[Ukiyo-e]] woodblock print by {{ill|Toyohara Chikanobu|en|Toyohara Chikanobu|qid=Q3087294|lt=Yōshū Chikanobu|1=Toyohara Chikanobu}}, 1890)]]
The {{nihongo3|"Magnificent/Exalted lineage"|華族|'''Kazoku'''}} was the hereditary {{ill|Peerage|en|Peerage|qid=Q51280089|lt=Peerage|1=Peerage}} of the {{ill|Empire of Japan|en|Empire of Japan|qid=Q188712|lt=Empire of Japan|1=Empire of Japan}}, which existed between 1869 and 1947. It was formed by merging the feudal lords (''[[Daimyo|daimyō]]'') and court nobles (''[[kuge]]'') into one system modelled after the [[:en:British peerage|British peerage]]. Distinguished military officers, politicians, and scholars were occasionally ennobled until the country's defeat in the {{ill|Pacific War|en|Pacific War|qid=Q184425|lt=Second World War|1=Pacific War}} in 1945 (新華族, ''shin kazoku'', lit. "the newly ennobled").<ref name="britannica">{{cite web| url=https://www.britannica.com/topic/kazoku |publisher=Encyclopaedia Britannica |title= Kazoku - Japanese nobility | date=Dec 21, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190831130049if_/https://www.britannica.com/topic/kazoku |archive-date=August 31, 2019}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=日本国語大辞典 |first=デジタル大辞泉,精選版 |title=新華族(シンカゾク)とは？ 意味や使い方 |url=https://kotobank.jp/word/%E6%96%B0%E8%8F%AF%E6%97%8F-536810 |access-date=2024-04-27 |website=コトバンク |language=ja}}</ref> The system was abolished with the {{ill|Constitution of Japan|en|Constitution of Japan|qid=Q237082|lt=1947 constitution|1=Constitution of Japan}}, which prohibited any form of aristocracy under it, but ''kazoku'' descendants still form the core of the traditional upper class in the country's society, distinct from the {{ill|nouveau riche|en|nouveau riche|qid=Q1898394|lt=nouveau riche|1=Nouveau riche}}.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2019-05-09 |title=THE LAST RETREAT OF JAPAN'S NOBILITY - The Washington Post |newspaper={{ill|The Washington Post|en|The Washington Post|qid=Q166032|lt=The Washington Post|1=The Washington Post}} |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/lifestyle/1997/05/21/the-last-retreat-of-japans-nobility/8fa34c94-e808-43eb-916d-3806924759bd/ |access-date=2024-04-27 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190509083044/https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/lifestyle/1997/05/21/the-last-retreat-of-japans-nobility/8fa34c94-e808-43eb-916d-3806924759bd/ |archive-date=2019-05-09 }}</ref>
'''Kazoku''' () should not be confused with ''"kazoku ()"'', which is pronounced the same in Japanese, but with a different character reading that means "immediate family" (as in the film ''[[:en:Kazoku (film)|Kazoku]]'' above).
== Origins ==
[[File:Prince Tokugawa Iesato.jpg|thumb|209x209px|Prince {{ill|Tokugawa Iesato|en|Tokugawa Iesato|qid=Q672741|lt=Tokugawa Iesato|1=Tokugawa Iesato}}, first head of the [[Tokugawa clan]] after the overthrow of the {{ill|Shogun|en|Shogun|qid=Q131767|lt=Shogun|1=Shogun}}, and was [[:en:President of the House of Peers|President of the House of Peers]] from 1903-1933.]]
Following the [[Meiji Restoration]] of 1868, the ancient court nobility of {{ill|Kyoto|en|Kyoto|qid=Q34600|lt=Kyoto|1=Kyoto}}, the {{nihongo||公家|1=Kuge|[[kuge]]}}, regained some of its lost status. Several members of the {{transliteration|ja|kuge}}, such as [[Iwakura Tomomi]] and {{ill|Nakayama Tadayasu|en|Nakayama Tadayasu|qid=Q1963991|lt=Nakayama Tadayasu|1=Nakayama Tadayasu}}, played a crucial role in the overthrow of the [[Tokugawa shogunate]],<ref>{{cite book|author=Peter Francis Kornicki|title=The emergence of the Meiji state|year=1998}}</ref>{{rp|115}} and the early {{ill|Government of Meiji Japan|en|Government of Meiji Japan|qid=Q1322181|lt=Government of Meiji Japan|1=Government of Meiji Japan}} nominated {{transliteration|ja|kuge}} to head all seven of the newly established administrative departments.
The {{ill|Meiji oligarchy|en|Meiji oligarchy|qid=Q1150742|lt=Meiji oligarchs|1=Meiji oligarchy}}, as part of their Westernizing reforms, merged the {{transliteration|ja|kuge}} with the former {{nihongo3|feudal lords|大名|[[:en:Daimyō|Daimyō]]}} into an expanded {{ill|Aristocracy (class)|en|Aristocracy (class)|qid=Q2478141|lt=aristocratic|1=Aristocracy (class)}} class on 25 July 1869, to recognize that the {{transliteration|ja|kuge}} and former {{transliteration|ja|daimyō}} were a social class distinct from the other designated social classes of {{nihongo3|former samurai|士族|{{ill|Shizoku|en|Shizoku|qid=Q3482406|lt=Shizoku|1=Shizoku}}}} and {{nihongo3|commoners|平民|heimin}}. They lost their territorial privileges.<ref name="britannica"/> [[Itō Hirobumi]], one of the principal authors of the [[:en:Meiji constitution|Meiji constitution]], intended the new {{transliteration|ja|kazoku}} peerage to serve as a political and social bulwark for the "restored" {{ill|Emperor of Japan|en|Emperor of Japan|qid=Q208233|lt=emperor|1=Emperor of Japan}} and the Japanese imperial institution. At the time, the {{transliteration|ja|kuge}} (142 families) and former {{transliteration|ja|daimyō}} (285 families) consisted of a group of total [[:en:List of Kuge families|427 families]].
[[File:Michitsune Koga 01.jpg|thumb|upright|Marquess [[Michitsune Koga]] (1842–1925), a member of the Imperial Family, descending from {{ill|Emperor Murakami|en|Emperor Murakami|qid=Q374015|lt=Emperor Murakami|1=Emperor Murakami}}.]]
All members of the {{transliteration|ja|kazoku}} without an official government appointment in the provinces were initially obliged to reside in {{ill|Tokyo|en|Tokyo|qid=Q1490|lt=Tokyo|1=Tokyo}}. By the end of 1869, a pension system was adopted, which gradually displaced the {{transliteration|ja|kazoku}} from their posts as provincial governors and as government leaders. The stipends promised by the government were eventually replaced by {{ill|Government bond|en|Government bond|qid=Q2324820|lt=Government bond|1=Government bond}}s.
== Development ==
In 1884 the {{transliteration|ja|kazoku}} were reorganized and the old feudal titles were replaced with:<ref name="britannica"/> # {{nihongo|[[Imperial Prince|Prince]], the equivalent of a European {{ill|Duke|en|Duke|qid=Q166886|lt=Duke|1=Duke}}|[[Wiktionary:公爵|公爵]]|Kōshaku}} # {{nihongo|[[Marquess]]|[[Wiktionary:侯爵|侯爵]]|Kōshaku}} # {{nihongo|{{ill|Count|en|Count|qid=Q3519259|lt=Count|1=Count}}, the equivalent of an {{ill|Earl|en|Earl|qid=Q1128240|lt=Earl|1=Earl}}|[[Wiktionary:伯爵|伯爵]]|Hakushaku}} # {{nihongo|{{ill|Viscount|en|Viscount|qid=Q185902|lt=Viscount|1=Viscount}}|[[Wiktionary:子爵|子爵]]|Shishaku}} # {{nihongo|{{ill|Baron|en|Baron|qid=Q165503|lt=Baron|1=Baron}}|[[Wiktionary:男爵|男爵]]|Danshaku}}
There were several categories within the {{transliteration|ja|kazoku}}. The initial Rank distribution for {{transliteration|ja|kazoku}} houses of {{transliteration|ja|kuge}} descent depended on the highest possible office to which its ancestors had been entitled in the imperial court. Thus, the heirs of the {{nihongo|{{ill|Five regent houses|en|Five regent houses|qid=Q1067142|lt=Five regent houses|1=Five regent houses}}||go-sekke}} of the [[Fujiwara clan|Fujiwara dynasty]] ({{ill|Konoe family|en|Konoe family|qid=Q1781840|lt=Konoe|1=Konoe family}}, {{ill|Takatsukasa family|en|Takatsukasa family|qid=Q846799|lt=Takatsukasa|1=Takatsukasa family}}, {{ill|Kujō family|en|Kujō family|qid=Q1791350|lt=Kujō|1=Kujō family}}, {{ill|Ichijō family|en|Ichijō family|qid=Q1535498|lt=Ichijō|1=Ichijō family}} and {{ill|Nijō family|en|Nijō family|qid=Q3065387|lt=Nijō|1=Nijō family}}) all became princes, the equivalent of a European {{ill|Duke|en|Duke|qid=Q166886|lt=Duke|1=Duke}}, upon the establishment of the {{transliteration|ja|kazoku}} in 1884.
The heads of eight other families ([[:en:Daigo family|Daigo]], [[:ja:広幡家|Hirohata]], [[:ja:菊亭家|Kikutei]], [[:en:Koga (kuge)|Koga]], {{ill|Saionji family|en|Saionji family|qid=Q7402472|lt=Saionji|1=Saionji family}}, [[:ja:徳大寺家|Tokudaiji]], [[:ja:大炊御門家|Ōinomikado]] and [[:ja:花山院家|Kasannoin]]) all with the Rank of {{transliteration|ja|[[:ja:清華家|seiga]]}}, the second Rank in the {{transliteration|ja|kuge}}, became marquesses at the same time. Those family heads in the third tier of the {{transliteration|ja|kuge}} and with the Rank of {{transliteration|ja|[[:ja:大臣家|daijin]]}} became counts. Heads of families in the lowest three tiers (those in the Ranks of {{transliteration|ja|[[:ja:羽林家|urin]]}}, {{transliteration|ja|[[:ja:名家|mei]]}} and {{transliteration|ja|[[:ja:半家|han]]}}) typically became viscounts, but could also be ennobled as counts.
Other appointments to the two highest Ranks in the {{transliteration|ja|kazoku}}—prince and marquess—from among the {{transliteration|ja|kuge}} were also made to reward certain {{transliteration|ja|kuge}} families for their roles in the [[Meiji Restoration]], for taking a prominent role in national affairs or for their close degree of relationship to the Imperial family. Thus the head of the {{transliteration|ja|seiga}}-Ranked {{ill|Sanjo family|lt=Sanjo|ja|三条家|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sanjo family|1=Sanjō family|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q4683560}} house became a prince in 1884. The heads of the Tokudaiji and the Saionji houses were advanced to the Rank of prince from the Rank of marquess in 1911 and 1920, respectively.
In recognition of his father's role in the [[Meiji Restoration]], [[Iwakura Tomosada]], the heir of noble [[Iwakura Tomomi]] and whose family had been in the fourth tier of {{transliteration|ja|kuge}} nobility, with the Rank of {{transliteration|ja|urin}}, was ennobled as a prince in 1884. {{ill|Nakayama Tadayasu|en|Nakayama Tadayasu|qid=Q1963991|lt=Nakayama Tadayasu|1=Nakayama Tadayasu}}, the {{ill|Emperor Meiji|en|Emperor Meiji|qid=Q174231|lt=Emperor Meiji|1=Emperor Meiji}}'s maternal grandfather and also from an {{transliteration|ja|urin}}-Ranked family, was ennobled as a marquess. The head of the [[:en:House of Second Shō|Shō family]], the former royal family of the [[:en:Ryūkyū Kingdom|Ryūkyū Kingdom]] ({{ill|Okinawa Prefecture|en|Okinawa Prefecture|qid=Q766445|lt=Okinawa|1=Okinawa Prefecture}}), was given the title of marquess. When the {{ill|Korean Empire|en|Korean Empire|qid=Q28233|lt=Korean Empire|1=Korean Empire}} was annexed in 1910, the {{ill|House of Yi|en|House of Yi|qid=Q626937|lt=House of Yi|1=House of Yi}} was {{ill|German mediatisation|en|German mediatisation|qid=Q314739|lt=mediatized|1=German mediatisation}} as an incorporated and therefore {{nihongo|subordinate kingship|王}}.
[[Image:Peers Club Inside.jpg|right|thumb|The interior of the [[Peers' Club]], Tokyo (1912). Unlike Western-style {{ill|gentlemen's club|en|gentlemen's club|qid=Q1236680|lt=gentlemen's club|1=Gentlemen's club}}s, membership was also open to women.]]
Excluding the [[Tokugawa clan|Tokugawa]]s, the initial {{transliteration|ja|kazoku}} Rank distribution for the former {{transliteration|ja|daimyō}} lords depended on rice revenue: those with 150,000 {{transliteration|ja|{{ill|Koku|en|Koku|qid=Q855048|lt=Koku|1=Koku}}}} or more became marquesses, those with 50,000 {{transliteration|ja|koku}} or more become counts, and those with holdings rated below 50,000 {{transliteration|ja|koku}} became viscounts. The head of the [[Tokugawa clan]], {{ill|Tokugawa Iesato|en|Tokugawa Iesato|qid=Q672741|lt=Tokugawa Iesato|1=Tokugawa Iesato}}, became a prince, the heads of primary Tokugawa branch houses ({{transliteration|ja|shinpan daimyō}}) became marquesses, the heads of the secondary branches became counts and the heads of more distant branches became viscounts. The head of the Matsudaira ({{ill|Fukui Domain|en|Fukui Domain|qid=Q903537|lt=Fukui Domain|1=Fukui Domain}}) branch was raised to the Rank of marquess from the Rank of count in 1888. In 1902, the former {{transliteration|ja|{{ill|Shogun|en|Shogun|qid=Q131767|lt=Shogun|1=Shogun}}}} [[Tokugawa Yoshinobu]] was created a prince, and the head of the Mito {{transliteration|ja|[[:en:Shinpan (daimyō)|shinpan]]}} house was raised to the same Rank, prince, in 1929.
Of the other former {{transliteration|ja|daimyō}} clans, the heads of the Mōri ({{ill|Chōshū Domain|en|Chōshū Domain|qid=Q876267|lt=Chōshū Domain|1=Chōshū Domain}}) and Shimazu ({{ill|Satsuma Domain|en|Satsuma Domain|qid=Q676187|lt=Satsuma Domain|1=Satsuma Domain}}) clans were both ennobled as princes in 1884 for their role in the Meiji Restoration; the Yamauchi ({{ill|Tosa Domain|en|Tosa Domain|qid=Q1189704|lt=Tosa Domain|1=Tosa Domain}}) clan was given the Rank of marquess. The heads of the main Asano ({{ill|Hiroshima Domain|en|Hiroshima Domain|qid=Q1141203|lt=Hiroshima Domain|1=Hiroshima Domain}}), Ikeda ({{ill|Okayama Domain|en|Okayama Domain|qid=Q903497|lt=Okayama|1=Okayama Domain}} and {{ill|Tottori Domain|en|Tottori Domain|qid=Q905521|lt=Tottori Domain|1=Tottori Domain}}s), Kuroda ({{ill|Fukuoka Domain|en|Fukuoka Domain|qid=Q208766|lt=Fukuoka Domain|1=Fukuoka Domain}}), Satake ({{ill|Kubota Domain|en|Kubota Domain|qid=Q1067720|lt=Kubota Domain|1=Kubota Domain}}), Nabeshima ({{ill|Saga Domain|en|Saga Domain|qid=Q2975995|lt=Saga Domain|1=Saga Domain}}), Hachisuka ({{ill|Tokushima Domain|en|Tokushima Domain|qid=Q3034557|lt=Tokushima Domain|1=Tokushima Domain}}), Hosokawa ({{ill|Kumamoto Domain|en|Kumamoto Domain|qid=Q1194248|lt=Kumamoto Domain|1=Kumamoto Domain}}) and Maeda ({{ill|Kaga Domain|en|Kaga Domain|qid=Q903448|lt=Kaga Domain|1=Kaga Domain}}) clans became marquesses in 1884.
[[File:ITŌ Hirobumi.jpg|thumb|231x231px|Japan's first Prime Minister [[Itō Hirobumi]], despite being born the son of an impoverished farmer, he was ennobled as prince.]]
Notably, the head of the main family line of the {{ill|Date clan|en|Date clan|qid=Q1151061|lt=Date clan|1=Date clan}}, which had formerly ruled the extensive {{ill|Sendai Domain|en|Sendai Domain|qid=Q1062182|lt=Sendai Domain|1=Sendai Domain}}, was only ennobled as a count and was thus denied a hereditary seat in the {{ill|House of Peers (Japan)|en|House of Peers (Japan)|qid=Q715139|lt=House of Peers|1=House of Peers (Japan)}}; this was likely due to the domain's prominent role as the leader of a coalition against the Imperial forces during the {{ill|Boshin War|en|Boshin War|qid=Q309184|lt=Boshin War|1=Boshin War}}. In 1891, the head of the Date-Uwajima family ({{ill|Uwajima Domain|en|Uwajima Domain|qid=Q994102|lt=Uwajima Domain|1=Uwajima Domain}}), a cadet branch of the clan which had remained loyal to the Emperor during the conflict, was raised to the Rank of marquess, having been ennobled as a count in 1884.
Many of those who had significant roles in the Meiji Restoration, or their heirs, were ennobled. [[:en:Ito Hirobumi|Ito Hirobumi]] and {{ill|Yamagata Aritomo|en|Yamagata Aritomo|qid=Q297636|lt=Yamagata Aritomo|1=Yamagata Aritomo}} were ennobled as counts in 1884, promoted to marquesses in 1895 and finally became princes in 1907. The heirs of [[:en:Okubo Toshimichi|Okubo Toshimichi]] and {{ill|Kido Takayoshi|en|Kido Takayoshi|qid=Q696402|lt=Kido Takayoshi|1=Kido Takayoshi}}, two of the [[:en:three great nobles|three great nobles]] of the Meiji Restoration, were ennobled as marquesses in 1884, followed by the heirs of samurai general-politician [[Saigō Takamori]] in 1902.
==Succession and numbers==
[[File:Kazoku-Japanese-Nobility-Group.png|thumb| part_of photo of ''Kazoku'' members'','' including Japan's prime minister before the {{ill|Pacific War|en|Pacific War|qid=Q184425|lt=Pacific War|1=Pacific War}}, {{ill|Fumimaro Konoe|en|Fumimaro Konoe|qid=Q315594|lt=Fumimaro Konoe|1=Fumimaro Konoe}} (1st row, far left)]]
As in the {{ill|Peerages in the United Kingdom|en|Peerages in the United Kingdom|qid=Q21488839|lt=British peerage|1=Peerages in the United Kingdom}}, only the actual holder of a title and his consort were considered members of the {{transliteration|ja|kazoku}}. The holders of the top two Ranks, prince and marquess, automatically became members of the {{ill|House of Peers (Japan)|en|House of Peers (Japan)|qid=Q715139|lt=House of Peers|1=House of Peers (Japan)}} in the {{ill|National Diet|en|National Diet|qid=Q202384|lt=Diet of Japan|1=National Diet}} upon their succession or upon majority (in the case of peers who were minors). Counts, viscounts and barons elected up to 150 representatives from their Ranks to sit in the House of Peers.
[[Image:Fumimaro Konoe President of the House of Peers.jpg|thumb|[[:en:Prince Konoe|Prince Konoe]] reading an [[:en:imperial rescript|imperial rescript]] as [[:en:President of the House of Peers|President of the House of Peers]], 1936]]
Under the [[Peerage Act of 7 July 1884]], pushed through by Home Minister and future first Prime Minister [[Itō Hirobumi]] after visiting {{ill|Europe|en|Europe|qid=Q46|lt=Europe|1=Europe}}, the Meiji government expanded the hereditary peerage with the award of {{transliteration|ja|kazoku}} status to persons regarded as having performed distinguished public services to the nation.<ref name="britannica"/> The government also divided the {{transliteration|ja|kazoku}} into five Ranks explicitly based on the [[:en:British peerage|British peerage]], but with titles deriving from the ancient {{ill|Chinese nobility|en|Chinese nobility|qid=Q2512388|lt=Chinese nobility|1=Chinese nobility}}.
Usually, though not always, titles and hereditary financial stipends passed according to {{ill|Primogeniture|en|Primogeniture|qid=Q250843|lt=Primogeniture|1=Primogeniture}}. Unlike in European peerage systems, but following traditional Japanese custom, illegitimate sons could succeed to titles and estates. To prevent their lineages from dying out, heads of {{transliteration|ja|kazoku}} houses could (and frequently did) adopt sons from collateral branches of their own houses, whether in the male or female lines of descent, and from other {{transliteration|ja|kazoku}} houses whether related or not.
Unlike European custom, the adopted heir of a peer could succeed to a title ahead of a more senior heir in terms of primogeniture. A 1904 amendment to the [[1889 Imperial Household Law]] allowed minor princes ({{transliteration|ja|{{ill|Ōke|en|Ōke|qid=Q864190|lt=ō|1=Ōke}}}}) of the {{ill|Imperial House of Japan|en|Imperial House of Japan|qid=Q909452|lt=imperial family|1=Imperial House of Japan}} to renounce their imperial status and become peers (in their own right) or heirs to childless peers. Initially there were 11 non-imperial princes, 24 marquesses, 76 counts, 324 viscounts and 74 barons, for a total of 509 peers.<ref>Jansen, ''The Making of Modern Japan''</ref>{{rp|391}} By 1928, through promotions and new creations, there were a total of 954 peers: 18 non-imperial princes, 40 marquesses, 108 counts, 379 viscounts and 409 barons. The {{transliteration|ja|kazoku}} reached a peak of 1016 {{ill|Japanese family|en|Japanese family|qid=Q3066141|lt=families|1=Japanese family}} in 1944.<ref>''{{ill|Kodansha Encyclopedia of Japan|en|Kodansha Encyclopedia of Japan|qid=Q488777|lt=Kodansha Encyclopedia of Japan|1=Kodansha Encyclopedia of Japan}}''</ref>{{rp|1194}}
The 1947 {{ill|Constitution of Japan|en|Constitution of Japan|qid=Q237082|lt=Constitution of Japan|1=Constitution of Japan}} abolished the {{transliteration|ja|kazoku}} and ended the use of all titles of nobility or Rank outside the immediate Imperial Family. Since the end of the war, many descendants of the {{transliteration|ja|kazoku}} families continue to occupy prominent roles in Japanese society and industry.<ref name="britannica"/><ref>Lebra, ''Above the Clouds: Status Culture of the Modern Japanese Nobility''.</ref>
The {{nihongo||華族会館|Kazoku Kaikan}}, or Peers' Club, was the association of the high nobility. It had its headquarters in the {{transliteration|ja|{{ill|Rokumeikan|en|Rokumeikan|qid=Q1039219|lt=Rokumeikan|1=Rokumeikan}}}} building. After 1947 it was renamed the {{nihongo||霞会館|{{ill|Kasumi Kaikan|en|Kasumi Kaikan|qid=Q11660821|lt=Kasumi Kaikan|1=Kasumi Kaikan}}}} and is located in the {{ill|Kasumigaseki Building|en|Kasumigaseki Building|qid=Q844780|lt=Kasumigaseki Building|1=Kasumigaseki Building}} in {{ill|Kasumigaseki|en|Kasumigaseki|qid=Q1268102|lt=Kasumigaseki|1=Kasumigaseki}}.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/lifestyle/1997/05/21/the-last-retreat-of-japans-nobility/8fa34c94-e808-43eb-916d-3806924759bd/|title=The Last Retreat of Japan's Nobility |first=Mary|last=Jordan|date=May 21, 1997|access-date=June 29, 2020|newspaper=Washington Post |via=www.washingtonpost.com |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190509083044/https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/lifestyle/1997/05/21/the-last-retreat-of-japans-nobility/8fa34c94-e808-43eb-916d-3806924759bd/ |archive-date=May 9, 2019}}</ref>
== Life ==
[[File:Mitsui Tsunamachi Club.jpg|thumb|Guest house of the {{ill|Mitsui family|en|Mitsui family|qid=Q950465|lt=Mitsui|1=Mitsui family}} Barony ({{ill|Mita, Minato, Tokyo|en|Mita, Minato, Tokyo|qid=Q3317048|lt=Mita, Tokyo|1=Mita, Minato, Tokyo}})]] Although ''kazoku'' families were supposed to live in a style that matched their status, living standards varied significantly from family to family. ''Kuge'' families, long having been seen as a spent force since the {{ill|Samurai|en|Samurai|qid=Q38142|lt=samurai class|1=Samurai}} became the de facto ruling class in the 11th century, tended to be significantly worse off than ''[[daimyo]]'' families. The ''Nara kazoku'' (奈良華族), consisting of 26 monk families from [[Kōfuku-ji|Kofukuji]], who descended from kuge families (22 of which belonged to the Fujiwara clan), were all made barons under the ''kazoku'' system. They were regarded as the poorest and received extra stipends to support their living.<ref>刑部芳則. "[https://cir.nii.ac.jp/crid/1521417756191974656 幕末・維新の青年群像 (第 3 回) 奈良華族の苦しい立場.]" ''青少年問題'' 60.春季 (2013): 52-57.</ref> A 1915 survey found that a kazoku family had around 13 servants on average, while the grandest families had hundreds.<ref>小田部雄次『華族 近代日本貴族の虚像と実像』中央公論新社〈中公新書1836〉、2006th year （平成18th year ）ISBN 978-4121018366, p. 65.</ref>
[[File:Bundesarchiv Bild 102-10281, Berlin, Prinz Takamatsu mit seiner Gattin.jpg|left|thumb|288x288px|{{ill|Nobuhito, Prince Takamatsu|en|Nobuhito, Prince Takamatsu|qid=Q1030368|lt=Prince|1=Nobuhito, Prince Takamatsu}} and {{ill|Kikuko, Princess Takamatsu|en|Kikuko, Princess Takamatsu|qid=Q467655|lt=Princess Takamatsu|1=Kikuko, Princess Takamatsu}} at the entrance of {{ill|Hotel Adlon|en|Hotel Adlon|qid=Q698095|lt=Hotel Adlon|1=Hotel Adlon}} in 1930]]
Almost all kazoku heirs raised in Japan attended {{ill|Gakushūin|en|Gakushūin|qid=Q1061900|lt=Gakushuin|1=Gakushūin}} for their primary and secondary education. For higher education, the most preferred institutions included the {{ill|University of Tokyo|en|University of Tokyo|qid=Q7842|lt=University of Tokyo|1=University of Tokyo}} (called Tokyo Imperial University 1897-1947) (e.g., Prince {{ill|Iemasa Tokugawa|en|Iemasa Tokugawa|qid=Q277171|lt=Iemasa Tokugawa|1=Iemasa Tokugawa}}, Count {{ill|Yoriyasu Arima|en|Yoriyasu Arima|qid=Q3572590|lt=Yoriyasu Arima|1=Yoriyasu Arima}}) and the {{ill|Imperial Japanese Naval Academy|en|Imperial Japanese Naval Academy|qid=Q2238519|lt=naval|1=Imperial Japanese Naval Academy}} and {{ill|Imperial Japanese Army Academy|en|Imperial Japanese Army Academy|qid=Q700130|lt=army academies|1=Imperial Japanese Army Academy}} (e.g., Viscount {{ill|Ogasawara Naganari|en|Ogasawara Naganari|qid=Q1150447|lt=Naganari Ogasawara|1=Ogasawara Naganari}}, Marquess {{ill|Toshinari Maeda|en|Toshinari Maeda|qid=Q3532631|lt=Toshinari Maeda|1=Toshinari Maeda}}).<ref>サトウユウキ, and 佐藤雄基. "[https://rikkyo.repo.nii.ac.jp/record/21252/files/AA11649321_20_08.pdf 卒業論文題目からみた近代歴史学の歩み: 東京帝国大学国史学科 1905-1944 の事例報告.]" ''立教大学日本学研究所年報'' 20 (2021): 49-30.</ref> Some opted to be educated overseas, such as at {{ill|Eton College|en|Eton College|qid=Q192088|lt=Eton College|1=Eton College}} (e.g., Prince {{ill|Tokugawa Iesato|en|Tokugawa Iesato|qid=Q672741|lt=Iesato Tokugawa|1=Tokugawa Iesato}}) and {{ill|University of Cambridge|en|University of Cambridge|qid=Q35794|lt=Cambridge University|1=University of Cambridge}} (e.g., Marquess {{ill|Masauji Hachisuka|en|Masauji Hachisuka|qid=Q11625684|lt=Masauji Hachisuka|1=Masauji Hachisuka}}, Baron {{ill|Koyata Iwasaki|en|Koyata Iwasaki|qid=Q5825501|lt=Koayata Iwasaki|1=Koyata Iwasaki}}). After completing their education, they pursued varied careers such as statesmen at the {{ill|House of Peers (Japan)|en|House of Peers (Japan)|qid=Q715139|lt=House of Peers|1=House of Peers (Japan)}}, diplomats (e.g., Prince {{ill|Iemasa Tokugawa|en|Iemasa Tokugawa|qid=Q277171|lt=Iemasa Tokugawa|1=Iemasa Tokugawa}}, Marquess {{ill|Nabeshima Naohiro (Saga)|en|Nabeshima Naohiro (Saga)|qid=Q5357768|lt=Naohiro Nabeshima|1=Nabeshima Naohiro (Saga)}}), and scholars (e.g., Marquess {{ill|Yoshichika Tokugawa|en|Yoshichika Tokugawa|qid=Q6636943|lt=Yoshichika Tokugawa|1=Yoshichika Tokugawa}}, Prince [[Tomohide Iwakura]]). Those who followed rather unusual career paths included Marquess {{ill|Yoshi Hijikata|en|Yoshi Hijikata|qid=Q1618018|lt=Hijikata Yoshi|1=Yoshi Hijikata}}, who became a communist and fled to {{ill|Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic|en|Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic|qid=Q2184|lt=Soviet Russia|1=Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic}}, and [[Meiho Ogasawara]], an heir to a viscountcy who pursued his passion for films and was disinherited in 1935.<ref>入倉友紀. "[https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/eizogaku/108/0/108_010809/_article/-char/ja/ 松竹蒲田撮影所における女性の映画製作への参画――女優兼脚本家, 松井千枝子の活動を通して.]" ''映像学'' 108 (2022): 144-163.</ref>
''Kazoku'' usually married within their class. The {{ill|Imperial Household Law|en|Imperial Household Law|qid=Q1324733|lt=Imperial Household Law|1=Imperial Household Law}} of 1889 prohibited Imperial Princes from marrying commoners, hence their options were limited to Princesses and daughters of ''kazoku'' families. ''Kazoku'' daughters who married into the Imperial family include {{ill|Kikuko, Princess Takamatsu|en|Kikuko, Princess Takamatsu|qid=Q467655|lt=Kikuko, Princess Takamatsu|1=Kikuko, Princess Takamatsu}} (née [[Tokugawa clan|Tokugawa]]), {{ill|Yuriko, Princess Mikasa|en|Yuriko, Princess Mikasa|qid=Q1189486|lt=Yuriko, Princess Mikasa|1=Yuriko, Princess Mikasa}} (née {{ill|Tannan Domain|en|Tannan Domain|qid=Q10863422|lt=Takagi|1=Tannan Domain}}), and {{ill|Setsuko, Princess Chichibu|en|Setsuko, Princess Chichibu|qid=Q3244162|lt=Setsuko, Princess Chichibu|1=Setsuko, Princess Chichibu}} (née {{ill|Matsudaira clan|en|Matsudaira clan|qid=Q1141077|lt=Matsudaira|1=Matsudaira clan}}).<gallery mode="packed"> File:Seiyokan (Nabeshima residence in Tokyo).jpg|Tokyo house of Marquess {{ill|Nabeshima Naohiro (Saga)|en|Nabeshima Naohiro (Saga)|qid=Q5357768|lt=Naohiro Nabeshima|1=Nabeshima Naohiro (Saga)}} File:Hofu Mouri Residence and Museum.JPG|Country house of Viscount [[Mototoshi Mori]] (now {{ill|Mōri Museum|en|Mōri Museum|qid=Q11547697|lt=Mori Museum|1=Mōri Museum}}) File:Former Maeda Estate 2009.jpg|Former residence of Marquess {{ill|Toshinari Maeda|en|Toshinari Maeda|qid=Q3532631|lt=Toshinari Maeda|1=Toshinari Maeda}} (now {{ill|Komaba Park|en|Komaba Park|qid=Q11668323|lt=Komaba Park|1=Komaba Park}}) File:View of Murin-an garden from main house.jpg|Former Kyoto House of Prince {{ill|Yamagata Aritomo|en|Yamagata Aritomo|qid=Q297636|lt=Aritomo Yamagata|1=Yamagata Aritomo}} File:Kazoku-Jogakko.JPG|Kazoku Girls' School ({{ill|Gakushūin|en|Gakushūin|qid=Q1061900|lt=Gakushuin|1=Gakushūin}} Girls' School) in 1889 File:Kaimei kizokuhyō by Shinsai.jpg|alt=Woodblock print by [[Kobayashi Toshimitsu]], "Table of Enlightened Aristocrats", 1877. Depicts {{ill|Prince Arisugawa Taruhito|en|Prince Arisugawa Taruhito|qid=Q668338|lt=Prince Arisugawa Taruhito|1=Prince Arisugawa Taruhito}}, {{ill|Enomoto Takeaki|en|Enomoto Takeaki|qid=Q532959|lt=Enomoto Takeaki|1=Enomoto Takeaki}}, {{ill|Ōkuma Shigenobu|en|Ōkuma Shigenobu|qid=Q243141|lt=Ōkuma Shigenobu|1=Ōkuma Shigenobu}}, {{ill|Kuroda Kiyotaka|en|Kuroda Kiyotaka|qid=Q714049|lt=Kuroda Kiyotaka|1=Kuroda Kiyotaka}}, [[Saigō Takamori]], {{ill|Yamagata Aritomo|en|Yamagata Aritomo|qid=Q297636|lt=Yamagata Aritomo|1=Yamagata Aritomo}}, [[Iwakura Tomomi]], [[Sanjō Sanetomi]], {{ill|Ōkubo Toshimichi|en|Ōkubo Toshimichi|qid=Q356118|lt=Ōkubo Toshimichi|1=Ōkubo Toshimichi}}, {{ill|Kido Takayoshi|en|Kido Takayoshi|qid=Q696402|lt=Kido Takayoshi|1=Kido Takayoshi}}, {{ill|Shimazu Hisamitsu|en|Shimazu Hisamitsu|qid=Q656135|lt=Shimazu Hisamitsu|1=Shimazu Hisamitsu}}, {{ill|Katsu Kaishū|en|Katsu Kaishū|qid=Q700470|lt=Katsu Kaishū|1=Katsu Kaishū}}, [[Itō Hirobumi]], {{ill|Kusumoto Masataka|en|Kusumoto Masataka|qid=Q11541218|lt=Kusumoto Masataka|1=Kusumoto Masataka}}, {{ill|Itagaki Taisuke|en|Itagaki Taisuke|qid=Q456380|lt=Itagaki Taisuke|1=Itagaki Taisuke}}, {{ill|Gotō Shōjirō|en|Gotō Shōjirō|qid=Q711721|lt=Gotō Shōjirō|1=Gotō Shōjirō}} and {{ill|Prince Komatsu Akihito|en|Prince Komatsu Akihito|qid=Q712627|lt=Prince Komatsu Akihito|1=Prince Komatsu Akihito}}|Woodblock print of "Enlightened Nobles", depicting prominent noble politicians and military commanders of the Meiji era, 1877 File:A0287992 2392942.jpg|[[Itsuko, Princess of Nashimoto]] (née Nabeshima) File:Emperor Shōwa (Hirohito) and Tsuneo Matsudaira aboard Battleship Musashi - 24 June 1943.jpg|{{ill|Tsuneo Matsudaira|en|Tsuneo Matsudaira|qid=Q4121055|lt=Tsuneo Matsudaira|1=Tsuneo Matsudaira}} and {{ill|Hirohito|en|Hirohito|qid=Q34479|lt=Emperor Hirohito|1=Hirohito}} on {{ill|Japanese battleship Musashi|en|Japanese battleship Musashi|qid=Q1127368|lt=Musashi|1=Japanese battleship Musashi}} File:Tokugawa Yoshichika 01.jpg|Marquess {{ill|Yoshichika Tokugawa|en|Yoshichika Tokugawa|qid=Q6636943|lt=Yoshichika Tokugawa|1=Yoshichika Tokugawa}} with a tiger he hunted in {{ill|British Malaya|en|British Malaya|qid=Q871091|lt=Malaya|1=British Malaya}} File:Princess Mikasa 2012-1-2.jpg|{{ill|Yuriko, Princess Mikasa|en|Yuriko, Princess Mikasa|qid=Q1189486|lt=Yuriko, Princess Mikasa|1=Yuriko, Princess Mikasa}}, one of the last members of the {{ill|Imperial House of Japan|en|Imperial House of Japan|qid=Q909452|lt=Imperial family|1=Imperial House of Japan}} who were born as ''kazoku'' File:Kijūrō Shidehara, Tomosaburō Katō and Iesato Tokugawa.jpg|Baron {{ill|Kijūrō Shidehara|en|Kijūrō Shidehara|qid=Q335191|lt=Kijuro Shidehara|1=Kijūrō Shidehara}} (later Prime Minister), Viscount {{ill|Katō Tomosaburō|en|Katō Tomosaburō|qid=Q335203|lt=Tomosaburo Kato|1=Katō Tomosaburō}} and Prince {{ill|Tokugawa Iesato|en|Tokugawa Iesato|qid=Q672741|lt=Iesato Tokugawa|1=Tokugawa Iesato}} at {{ill|Washington Naval Conference|en|Washington Naval Conference|qid=Q1050213|lt=Washington Naval Conference|1=Washington Naval Conference}} </gallery>

{{Short description|1869–1947 Japanese system of nobility}} {{For|the 1970 Japanese film|Kazoku (film)}} {{Italic title}}
[[File:Yōshū Chikanobu House of Peers.jpg|thumb|right|300px|The [[:en:House of Peers|House of Peers]] in session with {{ill|Emperor Meiji|en|Emperor Meiji|qid=Q174231|lt=Emperor Meiji|1=Emperor Meiji}} giving a speech. ([[Ukiyo-e]] woodblock print by {{ill|Toyohara Chikanobu|en|Toyohara Chikanobu|qid=Q3087294|lt=Yōshū Chikanobu|1=Toyohara Chikanobu}}, 1890)]]
The {{nihongo3|"Magnificent/Exalted lineage"|華族|'''Kazoku'''}} was the hereditary {{ill|Peerage|en|Peerage|qid=Q51280089|lt=Peerage|1=Peerage}} of the {{ill|Empire of Japan|en|Empire of Japan|qid=Q188712|lt=Empire of Japan|1=Empire of Japan}}, which existed between 1869 and 1947. It was formed by merging the feudal lords (''[[Daimyo|daimyō]]'') and court nobles (''[[kuge]]'') into one system modelled after the [[:en:British peerage|British peerage]]. Distinguished military officers, politicians, and scholars were occasionally ennobled until the country's defeat in the {{ill|Pacific War|en|Pacific War|qid=Q184425|lt=Second World War|1=Pacific War}} in 1945 (新華族, ''shin kazoku'', lit. "the newly ennobled").<ref name="britannica">{{cite web| url=https://www.britannica.com/topic/kazoku |publisher=Encyclopaedia Britannica |title= Kazoku - Japanese nobility | date=Dec 21, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190831130049if_/https://www.britannica.com/topic/kazoku |archive-date=August 31, 2019}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=日本国語大辞典 |first=デジタル大辞泉,精選版 |title=新華族(シンカゾク)とは？ 意味や使い方 |url=https://kotobank.jp/word/%E6%96%B0%E8%8F%AF%E6%97%8F-536810 |access-date=2024-04-27 |website=コトバンク |language=ja}}</ref> The system was abolished with the {{ill|Constitution of Japan|en|Constitution of Japan|qid=Q237082|lt=1947 constitution|1=Constitution of Japan}}, which prohibited any form of aristocracy under it, but ''kazoku'' descendants still form the core of the traditional upper class in the country's society, distinct from the {{ill|nouveau riche|en|nouveau riche|qid=Q1898394|lt=nouveau riche|1=Nouveau riche}}.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2019-05-09 |title=THE LAST RETREAT OF JAPAN'S NOBILITY - The Washington Post |newspaper={{ill|The Washington Post|en|The Washington Post|qid=Q166032|lt=The Washington Post|1=The Washington Post}} |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/lifestyle/1997/05/21/the-last-retreat-of-japans-nobility/8fa34c94-e808-43eb-916d-3806924759bd/ |access-date=2024-04-27 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190509083044/https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/lifestyle/1997/05/21/the-last-retreat-of-japans-nobility/8fa34c94-e808-43eb-916d-3806924759bd/ |archive-date=2019-05-09 }}</ref>
'''Kazoku''' () should not be confused with ''"kazoku ()"'', which is pronounced the same in Japanese, but with a different character reading that means "immediate family" (as in the film ''[[:en:Kazoku (film)|Kazoku]]'' above).
== Origins ==
[[File:Prince Tokugawa Iesato.jpg|thumb|209x209px|Prince {{ill|Tokugawa Iesato|en|Tokugawa Iesato|qid=Q672741|lt=Tokugawa Iesato|1=Tokugawa Iesato}}, first head of the [[Tokugawa clan]] after the overthrow of the {{ill|Shogun|en|Shogun|qid=Q131767|lt=Shogun|1=Shogun}}, and was [[:en:President of the House of Peers|President of the House of Peers]] from 1903-1933.]]
Following the [[Meiji Restoration]] of 1868, the ancient court nobility of {{ill|Kyoto|en|Kyoto|qid=Q34600|lt=Kyoto|1=Kyoto}}, the {{nihongo||公家|1=Kuge|[[kuge]]}}, regained some of its lost status. Several members of the {{transliteration|ja|kuge}}, such as [[Iwakura Tomomi]] and {{ill|Nakayama Tadayasu|en|Nakayama Tadayasu|qid=Q1963991|lt=Nakayama Tadayasu|1=Nakayama Tadayasu}}, played a crucial role in the overthrow of the [[Tokugawa shogunate]],<ref>{{cite book|author=Peter Francis Kornicki|title=The emergence of the Meiji state|year=1998}}</ref>{{rp|115}} and the early {{ill|Government of Meiji Japan|en|Government of Meiji Japan|qid=Q1322181|lt=Government of Meiji Japan|1=Government of Meiji Japan}} nominated {{transliteration|ja|kuge}} to head all seven of the newly established administrative departments.
The {{ill|Meiji oligarchy|en|Meiji oligarchy|qid=Q1150742|lt=Meiji oligarchs|1=Meiji oligarchy}}, as part of their Westernizing reforms, merged the {{transliteration|ja|kuge}} with the former {{nihongo3|feudal lords|大名|[[:en:Daimyō|Daimyō]]}} into an expanded {{ill|Aristocracy (class)|en|Aristocracy (class)|qid=Q2478141|lt=aristocratic|1=Aristocracy (class)}} class on 25 July 1869, to recognize that the {{transliteration|ja|kuge}} and former {{transliteration|ja|daimyō}} were a social class distinct from the other designated social classes of {{nihongo3|former samurai|士族|{{ill|Shizoku|en|Shizoku|qid=Q3482406|lt=Shizoku|1=Shizoku}}}} and {{nihongo3|commoners|平民|heimin}}. They lost their territorial privileges.<ref name="britannica"/> [[Itō Hirobumi]], one of the principal authors of the [[:en:Meiji constitution|Meiji constitution]], intended the new {{transliteration|ja|kazoku}} peerage to serve as a political and social bulwark for the "restored" {{ill|Emperor of Japan|en|Emperor of Japan|qid=Q208233|lt=emperor|1=Emperor of Japan}} and the Japanese imperial institution. At the time, the {{transliteration|ja|kuge}} (142 families) and former {{transliteration|ja|daimyō}} (285 families) consisted of a group of total [[:en:List of Kuge families|427 families]].
[[File:Michitsune Koga 01.jpg|thumb|upright|Marquess [[Michitsune Koga]] (1842–1925), a member of the Imperial Family, descending from {{ill|Emperor Murakami|en|Emperor Murakami|qid=Q374015|lt=Emperor Murakami|1=Emperor Murakami}}.]]
All members of the {{transliteration|ja|kazoku}} without an official government appointment in the provinces were initially obliged to reside in {{ill|Tokyo|en|Tokyo|qid=Q1490|lt=Tokyo|1=Tokyo}}. By the end of 1869, a pension system was adopted, which gradually displaced the {{transliteration|ja|kazoku}} from their posts as provincial governors and as government leaders. The stipends promised by the government were eventually replaced by {{ill|Government bond|en|Government bond|qid=Q2324820|lt=Government bond|1=Government bond}}s.
== Development ==
In 1884 the {{transliteration|ja|kazoku}} were reorganized and the old feudal titles were replaced with:<ref name="britannica"/> # {{nihongo|[[Imperial Prince|Prince]], the equivalent of a European {{ill|Duke|en|Duke|qid=Q166886|lt=Duke|1=Duke}}|[[Wiktionary:公爵|公爵]]|Kōshaku}} # {{nihongo|[[Marquess]]|[[Wiktionary:侯爵|侯爵]]|Kōshaku}} # {{nihongo|{{ill|Count|en|Count|qid=Q3519259|lt=Count|1=Count}}, the equivalent of an {{ill|Earl|en|Earl|qid=Q1128240|lt=Earl|1=Earl}}|[[Wiktionary:伯爵|伯爵]]|Hakushaku}} # {{nihongo|{{ill|Viscount|en|Viscount|qid=Q185902|lt=Viscount|1=Viscount}}|[[Wiktionary:子爵|子爵]]|Shishaku}} # {{nihongo|{{ill|Baron|en|Baron|qid=Q165503|lt=Baron|1=Baron}}|[[Wiktionary:男爵|男爵]]|Danshaku}}
There were several categories within the {{transliteration|ja|kazoku}}. The initial Rank distribution for {{transliteration|ja|kazoku}} houses of {{transliteration|ja|kuge}} descent depended on the highest possible office to which its ancestors had been entitled in the imperial court. Thus, the heirs of the {{nihongo|{{ill|Five regent houses|en|Five regent houses|qid=Q1067142|lt=Five regent houses|1=Five regent houses}}||go-sekke}} of the [[Fujiwara clan|Fujiwara dynasty]] ({{ill|Konoe family|en|Konoe family|qid=Q1781840|lt=Konoe|1=Konoe family}}, {{ill|Takatsukasa family|en|Takatsukasa family|qid=Q846799|lt=Takatsukasa|1=Takatsukasa family}}, {{ill|Kujō family|en|Kujō family|qid=Q1791350|lt=Kujō|1=Kujō family}}, {{ill|Ichijō family|en|Ichijō family|qid=Q1535498|lt=Ichijō|1=Ichijō family}} and {{ill|Nijō family|en|Nijō family|qid=Q3065387|lt=Nijō|1=Nijō family}}) all became princes, the equivalent of a European {{ill|Duke|en|Duke|qid=Q166886|lt=Duke|1=Duke}}, upon the establishment of the {{transliteration|ja|kazoku}} in 1884.
The heads of eight other families ([[:en:Daigo family|Daigo]], [[:ja:広幡家|Hirohata]], [[:ja:菊亭家|Kikutei]], [[:en:Koga (kuge)|Koga]], {{ill|Saionji family|en|Saionji family|qid=Q7402472|lt=Saionji|1=Saionji family}}, [[:ja:徳大寺家|Tokudaiji]], [[:ja:大炊御門家|Ōinomikado]] and [[:ja:花山院家|Kasannoin]]) all with the Rank of {{transliteration|ja|[[:ja:清華家|seiga]]}}, the second Rank in the {{transliteration|ja|kuge}}, became marquesses at the same time. Those family heads in the third tier of the {{transliteration|ja|kuge}} and with the Rank of {{transliteration|ja|[[:ja:大臣家|daijin]]}} became counts. Heads of families in the lowest three tiers (those in the Ranks of {{transliteration|ja|[[:ja:羽林家|urin]]}}, {{transliteration|ja|[[:ja:名家|mei]]}} and {{transliteration|ja|[[:ja:半家|han]]}}) typically became viscounts, but could also be ennobled as counts.
Other appointments to the two highest Ranks in the {{transliteration|ja|kazoku}}—prince and marquess—from among the {{transliteration|ja|kuge}} were also made to reward certain {{transliteration|ja|kuge}} families for their roles in the [[Meiji Restoration]], for taking a prominent role in national affairs or for their close degree of relationship to the Imperial family. Thus the head of the {{transliteration|ja|seiga}}-Ranked {{ill|Sanjo family|lt=Sanjo|ja|三条家|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sanjo family|1=Sanjō family|comment=changed title based on wikidata|qid=Q4683560}} house became a prince in 1884. The heads of the Tokudaiji and the Saionji houses were advanced to the Rank of prince from the Rank of marquess in 1911 and 1920, respectively.
In recognition of his father's role in the [[Meiji Restoration]], [[Iwakura Tomosada]], the heir of noble [[Iwakura Tomomi]] and whose family had been in the fourth tier of {{transliteration|ja|kuge}} nobility, with the Rank of {{transliteration|ja|urin}}, was ennobled as a prince in 1884. {{ill|Nakayama Tadayasu|en|Nakayama Tadayasu|qid=Q1963991|lt=Nakayama Tadayasu|1=Nakayama Tadayasu}}, the {{ill|Emperor Meiji|en|Emperor Meiji|qid=Q174231|lt=Emperor Meiji|1=Emperor Meiji}}'s maternal grandfather and also from an {{transliteration|ja|urin}}-Ranked family, was ennobled as a marquess. The head of the [[:en:House of Second Shō|Shō family]], the former royal family of the [[:en:Ryūkyū Kingdom|Ryūkyū Kingdom]] ({{ill|Okinawa Prefecture|en|Okinawa Prefecture|qid=Q766445|lt=Okinawa|1=Okinawa Prefecture}}), was given the title of marquess. When the {{ill|Korean Empire|en|Korean Empire|qid=Q28233|lt=Korean Empire|1=Korean Empire}} was annexed in 1910, the {{ill|House of Yi|en|House of Yi|qid=Q626937|lt=House of Yi|1=House of Yi}} was {{ill|German mediatisation|en|German mediatisation|qid=Q314739|lt=mediatized|1=German mediatisation}} as an incorporated and therefore {{nihongo|subordinate kingship|王}}.
[[Image:Peers Club Inside.jpg|right|thumb|The interior of the [[Peers' Club]], Tokyo (1912). Unlike Western-style {{ill|gentlemen's club|en|gentlemen's club|qid=Q1236680|lt=gentlemen's club|1=Gentlemen's club}}s, membership was also open to women.]]
Excluding the [[Tokugawa clan|Tokugawa]]s, the initial {{transliteration|ja|kazoku}} Rank distribution for the former {{transliteration|ja|daimyō}} lords depended on rice revenue: those with 150,000 {{transliteration|ja|{{ill|Koku|en|Koku|qid=Q855048|lt=Koku|1=Koku}}}} or more became marquesses, those with 50,000 {{transliteration|ja|koku}} or more become counts, and those with holdings rated below 50,000 {{transliteration|ja|koku}} became viscounts. The head of the [[Tokugawa clan]], {{ill|Tokugawa Iesato|en|Tokugawa Iesato|qid=Q672741|lt=Tokugawa Iesato|1=Tokugawa Iesato}}, became a prince, the heads of primary Tokugawa branch houses ({{transliteration|ja|shinpan daimyō}}) became marquesses, the heads of the secondary branches became counts and the heads of more distant branches became viscounts. The head of the Matsudaira ({{ill|Fukui Domain|en|Fukui Domain|qid=Q903537|lt=Fukui Domain|1=Fukui Domain}}) branch was raised to the Rank of marquess from the Rank of count in 1888. In 1902, the former {{transliteration|ja|{{ill|Shogun|en|Shogun|qid=Q131767|lt=Shogun|1=Shogun}}}} [[Tokugawa Yoshinobu]] was created a prince, and the head of the Mito {{transliteration|ja|[[:en:Shinpan (daimyō)|shinpan]]}} house was raised to the same Rank, prince, in 1929.
Of the other former {{transliteration|ja|daimyō}} clans, the heads of the Mōri ({{ill|Chōshū Domain|en|Chōshū Domain|qid=Q876267|lt=Chōshū Domain|1=Chōshū Domain}}) and Shimazu ({{ill|Satsuma Domain|en|Satsuma Domain|qid=Q676187|lt=Satsuma Domain|1=Satsuma Domain}}) clans were both ennobled as princes in 1884 for their role in the Meiji Restoration; the Yamauchi ({{ill|Tosa Domain|en|Tosa Domain|qid=Q1189704|lt=Tosa Domain|1=Tosa Domain}}) clan was given the Rank of marquess. The heads of the main Asano ({{ill|Hiroshima Domain|en|Hiroshima Domain|qid=Q1141203|lt=Hiroshima Domain|1=Hiroshima Domain}}), Ikeda ({{ill|Okayama Domain|en|Okayama Domain|qid=Q903497|lt=Okayama|1=Okayama Domain}} and {{ill|Tottori Domain|en|Tottori Domain|qid=Q905521|lt=Tottori Domain|1=Tottori Domain}}s), Kuroda ({{ill|Fukuoka Domain|en|Fukuoka Domain|qid=Q208766|lt=Fukuoka Domain|1=Fukuoka Domain}}), Satake ({{ill|Kubota Domain|en|Kubota Domain|qid=Q1067720|lt=Kubota Domain|1=Kubota Domain}}), Nabeshima ({{ill|Saga Domain|en|Saga Domain|qid=Q2975995|lt=Saga Domain|1=Saga Domain}}), Hachisuka ({{ill|Tokushima Domain|en|Tokushima Domain|qid=Q3034557|lt=Tokushima Domain|1=Tokushima Domain}}), Hosokawa ({{ill|Kumamoto Domain|en|Kumamoto Domain|qid=Q1194248|lt=Kumamoto Domain|1=Kumamoto Domain}}) and Maeda ({{ill|Kaga Domain|en|Kaga Domain|qid=Q903448|lt=Kaga Domain|1=Kaga Domain}}) clans became marquesses in 1884.
[[File:ITŌ Hirobumi.jpg|thumb|231x231px|Japan's first Prime Minister [[Itō Hirobumi]], despite being born the son of an impoverished farmer, he was ennobled as prince.]]
Notably, the head of the main family line of the {{ill|Date clan|en|Date clan|qid=Q1151061|lt=Date clan|1=Date clan}}, which had formerly ruled the extensive {{ill|Sendai Domain|en|Sendai Domain|qid=Q1062182|lt=Sendai Domain|1=Sendai Domain}}, was only ennobled as a count and was thus denied a hereditary seat in the {{ill|House of Peers (Japan)|en|House of Peers (Japan)|qid=Q715139|lt=House of Peers|1=House of Peers (Japan)}}; this was likely due to the domain's prominent role as the leader of a coalition against the Imperial forces during the {{ill|Boshin War|en|Boshin War|qid=Q309184|lt=Boshin War|1=Boshin War}}. In 1891, the head of the Date-Uwajima family ({{ill|Uwajima Domain|en|Uwajima Domain|qid=Q994102|lt=Uwajima Domain|1=Uwajima Domain}}), a cadet branch of the clan which had remained loyal to the Emperor during the conflict, was raised to the Rank of marquess, having been ennobled as a count in 1884.
Many of those who had significant roles in the Meiji Restoration, or their heirs, were ennobled. [[:en:Ito Hirobumi|Ito Hirobumi]] and {{ill|Yamagata Aritomo|en|Yamagata Aritomo|qid=Q297636|lt=Yamagata Aritomo|1=Yamagata Aritomo}} were ennobled as counts in 1884, promoted to marquesses in 1895 and finally became princes in 1907. The heirs of [[:en:Okubo Toshimichi|Okubo Toshimichi]] and {{ill|Kido Takayoshi|en|Kido Takayoshi|qid=Q696402|lt=Kido Takayoshi|1=Kido Takayoshi}}, two of the [[:en:three great nobles|three great nobles]] of the Meiji Restoration, were ennobled as marquesses in 1884, followed by the heirs of samurai general-politician [[Saigō Takamori]] in 1902.
==Succession and numbers==
[[File:Kazoku-Japanese-Nobility-Group.png|thumb| part_of photo of ''Kazoku'' members'','' including Japan's prime minister before the {{ill|Pacific War|en|Pacific War|qid=Q184425|lt=Pacific War|1=Pacific War}}, {{ill|Fumimaro Konoe|en|Fumimaro Konoe|qid=Q315594|lt=Fumimaro Konoe|1=Fumimaro Konoe}} (1st row, far left)]]
As in the {{ill|Peerages in the United Kingdom|en|Peerages in the United Kingdom|qid=Q21488839|lt=British peerage|1=Peerages in the United Kingdom}}, only the actual holder of a title and his consort were considered members of the {{transliteration|ja|kazoku}}. The holders of the top two Ranks, prince and marquess, automatically became members of the {{ill|House of Peers (Japan)|en|House of Peers (Japan)|qid=Q715139|lt=House of Peers|1=House of Peers (Japan)}} in the {{ill|National Diet|en|National Diet|qid=Q202384|lt=Diet of Japan|1=National Diet}} upon their succession or upon majority (in the case of peers who were minors). Counts, viscounts and barons elected up to 150 representatives from their Ranks to sit in the House of Peers.
[[Image:Fumimaro Konoe President of the House of Peers.jpg|thumb|[[:en:Prince Konoe|Prince Konoe]] reading an [[:en:imperial rescript|imperial rescript]] as [[:en:President of the House of Peers|President of the House of Peers]], 1936]]
Under the [[Peerage Act of 7 July 1884]], pushed through by Home Minister and future first Prime Minister [[Itō Hirobumi]] after visiting {{ill|Europe|en|Europe|qid=Q46|lt=Europe|1=Europe}}, the Meiji government expanded the hereditary peerage with the award of {{transliteration|ja|kazoku}} status to persons regarded as having performed distinguished public services to the nation.<ref name="britannica"/> The government also divided the {{transliteration|ja|kazoku}} into five Ranks explicitly based on the [[:en:British peerage|British peerage]], but with titles deriving from the ancient {{ill|Chinese nobility|en|Chinese nobility|qid=Q2512388|lt=Chinese nobility|1=Chinese nobility}}.
Usually, though not always, titles and hereditary financial stipends passed according to {{ill|Primogeniture|en|Primogeniture|qid=Q250843|lt=Primogeniture|1=Primogeniture}}. Unlike in European peerage systems, but following traditional Japanese custom, illegitimate sons could succeed to titles and estates. To prevent their lineages from dying out, heads of {{transliteration|ja|kazoku}} houses could (and frequently did) adopt sons from collateral branches of their own houses, whether in the male or female lines of descent, and from other {{transliteration|ja|kazoku}} houses whether related or not.
Unlike European custom, the adopted heir of a peer could succeed to a title ahead of a more senior heir in terms of primogeniture. A 1904 amendment to the [[1889 Imperial Household Law]] allowed minor princes ({{transliteration|ja|{{ill|Ōke|en|Ōke|qid=Q864190|lt=ō|1=Ōke}}}}) of the {{ill|Imperial House of Japan|en|Imperial House of Japan|qid=Q909452|lt=imperial family|1=Imperial House of Japan}} to renounce their imperial status and become peers (in their own right) or heirs to childless peers. Initially there were 11 non-imperial princes, 24 marquesses, 76 counts, 324 viscounts and 74 barons, for a total of 509 peers.<ref>Jansen, ''The Making of Modern Japan''</ref>{{rp|391}} By 1928, through promotions and new creations, there were a total of 954 peers: 18 non-imperial princes, 40 marquesses, 108 counts, 379 viscounts and 409 barons. The {{transliteration|ja|kazoku}} reached a peak of 1016 {{ill|Japanese family|en|Japanese family|qid=Q3066141|lt=families|1=Japanese family}} in 1944.<ref>''{{ill|Kodansha Encyclopedia of Japan|en|Kodansha Encyclopedia of Japan|qid=Q488777|lt=Kodansha Encyclopedia of Japan|1=Kodansha Encyclopedia of Japan}}''</ref>{{rp|1194}}
The 1947 {{ill|Constitution of Japan|en|Constitution of Japan|qid=Q237082|lt=Constitution of Japan|1=Constitution of Japan}} abolished the {{transliteration|ja|kazoku}} and ended the use of all titles of nobility or Rank outside the immediate Imperial Family. Since the end of the war, many descendants of the {{transliteration|ja|kazoku}} families continue to occupy prominent roles in Japanese society and industry.<ref name="britannica"/><ref>Lebra, ''Above the Clouds: Status Culture of the Modern Japanese Nobility''.</ref>
The {{nihongo||華族会館|Kazoku Kaikan}}, or Peers' Club, was the association of the high nobility. It had its headquarters in the {{transliteration|ja|{{ill|Rokumeikan|en|Rokumeikan|qid=Q1039219|lt=Rokumeikan|1=Rokumeikan}}}} building. After 1947 it was renamed the {{nihongo||霞会館|{{ill|Kasumi Kaikan|en|Kasumi Kaikan|qid=Q11660821|lt=Kasumi Kaikan|1=Kasumi Kaikan}}}} and is located in the {{ill|Kasumigaseki Building|en|Kasumigaseki Building|qid=Q844780|lt=Kasumigaseki Building|1=Kasumigaseki Building}} in {{ill|Kasumigaseki|en|Kasumigaseki|qid=Q1268102|lt=Kasumigaseki|1=Kasumigaseki}}.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/lifestyle/1997/05/21/the-last-retreat-of-japans-nobility/8fa34c94-e808-43eb-916d-3806924759bd/|title=The Last Retreat of Japan's Nobility |first=Mary|last=Jordan|date=May 21, 1997|access-date=June 29, 2020|newspaper=Washington Post |via=www.washingtonpost.com |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190509083044/https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/lifestyle/1997/05/21/the-last-retreat-of-japans-nobility/8fa34c94-e808-43eb-916d-3806924759bd/ |archive-date=May 9, 2019}}</ref>
== Life ==
[[File:Mitsui Tsunamachi Club.jpg|thumb|Guest house of the {{ill|Mitsui family|en|Mitsui family|qid=Q950465|lt=Mitsui|1=Mitsui family}} Barony ({{ill|Mita, Minato, Tokyo|en|Mita, Minato, Tokyo|qid=Q3317048|lt=Mita, Tokyo|1=Mita, Minato, Tokyo}})]] Although ''kazoku'' families were supposed to live in a style that matched their status, living standards varied significantly from family to family. ''Kuge'' families, long having been seen as a spent force since the {{ill|Samurai|en|Samurai|qid=Q38142|lt=samurai class|1=Samurai}} became the de facto ruling class in the 11th century, tended to be significantly worse off than ''[[daimyo]]'' families. The ''Nara kazoku'' (奈良華族), consisting of 26 monk families from [[Kōfuku-ji|Kofukuji]], who descended from kuge families (22 of which belonged to the Fujiwara clan), were all made barons under the ''kazoku'' system. They were regarded as the poorest and received extra stipends to support their living.<ref>刑部芳則. "[https://cir.nii.ac.jp/crid/1521417756191974656 幕末・維新の青年群像 (第 3 回) 奈良華族の苦しい立場.]" ''青少年問題'' 60.春季 (2013): 52-57.</ref> A 1915 survey found that a kazoku family had around 13 servants on average, while the grandest families had hundreds.<ref>小田部雄次『華族 近代日本貴族の虚像と実像』中央公論新社〈中公新書1836〉、2006th year （平成18th year ）ISBN 978-4121018366, p. 65.</ref>
[[File:Bundesarchiv Bild 102-10281, Berlin, Prinz Takamatsu mit seiner Gattin.jpg|left|thumb|288x288px|{{ill|Nobuhito, Prince Takamatsu|en|Nobuhito, Prince Takamatsu|qid=Q1030368|lt=Prince|1=Nobuhito, Prince Takamatsu}} and {{ill|Kikuko, Princess Takamatsu|en|Kikuko, Princess Takamatsu|qid=Q467655|lt=Princess Takamatsu|1=Kikuko, Princess Takamatsu}} at the entrance of {{ill|Hotel Adlon|en|Hotel Adlon|qid=Q698095|lt=Hotel Adlon|1=Hotel Adlon}} in 1930]]
Almost all kazoku heirs raised in Japan attended {{ill|Gakushūin|en|Gakushūin|qid=Q1061900|lt=Gakushuin|1=Gakushūin}} for their primary and secondary education. For higher education, the most preferred institutions included the {{ill|University of Tokyo|en|University of Tokyo|qid=Q7842|lt=University of Tokyo|1=University of Tokyo}} (called Tokyo Imperial University 1897-1947) (e.g., Prince {{ill|Iemasa Tokugawa|en|Iemasa Tokugawa|qid=Q277171|lt=Iemasa Tokugawa|1=Iemasa Tokugawa}}, Count {{ill|Yoriyasu Arima|en|Yoriyasu Arima|qid=Q3572590|lt=Yoriyasu Arima|1=Yoriyasu Arima}}) and the {{ill|Imperial Japanese Naval Academy|en|Imperial Japanese Naval Academy|qid=Q2238519|lt=naval|1=Imperial Japanese Naval Academy}} and {{ill|Imperial Japanese Army Academy|en|Imperial Japanese Army Academy|qid=Q700130|lt=army academies|1=Imperial Japanese Army Academy}} (e.g., Viscount {{ill|Ogasawara Naganari|en|Ogasawara Naganari|qid=Q1150447|lt=Naganari Ogasawara|1=Ogasawara Naganari}}, Marquess {{ill|Toshinari Maeda|en|Toshinari Maeda|qid=Q3532631|lt=Toshinari Maeda|1=Toshinari Maeda}}).<ref>サトウユウキ, and 佐藤雄基. "[https://rikkyo.repo.nii.ac.jp/record/21252/files/AA11649321_20_08.pdf 卒業論文題目からみた近代歴史学の歩み: 東京帝国大学国史学科 1905-1944 の事例報告.]" ''立教大学日本学研究所年報'' 20 (2021): 49-30.</ref> Some opted to be educated overseas, such as at {{ill|Eton College|en|Eton College|qid=Q192088|lt=Eton College|1=Eton College}} (e.g., Prince {{ill|Tokugawa Iesato|en|Tokugawa Iesato|qid=Q672741|lt=Iesato Tokugawa|1=Tokugawa Iesato}}) and {{ill|University of Cambridge|en|University of Cambridge|qid=Q35794|lt=Cambridge University|1=University of Cambridge}} (e.g., Marquess {{ill|Masauji Hachisuka|en|Masauji Hachisuka|qid=Q11625684|lt=Masauji Hachisuka|1=Masauji Hachisuka}}, Baron {{ill|Koyata Iwasaki|en|Koyata Iwasaki|qid=Q5825501|lt=Koayata Iwasaki|1=Koyata Iwasaki}}). After completing their education, they pursued varied careers such as statesmen at the {{ill|House of Peers (Japan)|en|House of Peers (Japan)|qid=Q715139|lt=House of Peers|1=House of Peers (Japan)}}, diplomats (e.g., Prince {{ill|Iemasa Tokugawa|en|Iemasa Tokugawa|qid=Q277171|lt=Iemasa Tokugawa|1=Iemasa Tokugawa}}, Marquess {{ill|Nabeshima Naohiro (Saga)|en|Nabeshima Naohiro (Saga)|qid=Q5357768|lt=Naohiro Nabeshima|1=Nabeshima Naohiro (Saga)}}), and scholars (e.g., Marquess {{ill|Yoshichika Tokugawa|en|Yoshichika Tokugawa|qid=Q6636943|lt=Yoshichika Tokugawa|1=Yoshichika Tokugawa}}, Prince [[Tomohide Iwakura]]). Those who followed rather unusual career paths included Marquess {{ill|Yoshi Hijikata|en|Yoshi Hijikata|qid=Q1618018|lt=Hijikata Yoshi|1=Yoshi Hijikata}}, who became a communist and fled to {{ill|Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic|en|Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic|qid=Q2184|lt=Soviet Russia|1=Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic}}, and [[Meiho Ogasawara]], an heir to a viscountcy who pursued his passion for films and was disinherited in 1935.<ref>入倉友紀. "[https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/eizogaku/108/0/108_010809/_article/-char/ja/ 松竹蒲田撮影所における女性の映画製作への参画――女優兼脚本家, 松井千枝子の活動を通して.]" ''映像学'' 108 (2022): 144-163.</ref>
''Kazoku'' usually married within their class. The {{ill|Imperial Household Law|en|Imperial Household Law|qid=Q1324733|lt=Imperial Household Law|1=Imperial Household Law}} of 1889 prohibited Imperial Princes from marrying commoners, hence their options were limited to Princesses and daughters of ''kazoku'' families. ''Kazoku'' daughters who married into the Imperial family include {{ill|Kikuko, Princess Takamatsu|en|Kikuko, Princess Takamatsu|qid=Q467655|lt=Kikuko, Princess Takamatsu|1=Kikuko, Princess Takamatsu}} (née [[Tokugawa clan|Tokugawa]]), {{ill|Yuriko, Princess Mikasa|en|Yuriko, Princess Mikasa|qid=Q1189486|lt=Yuriko, Princess Mikasa|1=Yuriko, Princess Mikasa}} (née {{ill|Tannan Domain|en|Tannan Domain|qid=Q10863422|lt=Takagi|1=Tannan Domain}}), and {{ill|Setsuko, Princess Chichibu|en|Setsuko, Princess Chichibu|qid=Q3244162|lt=Setsuko, Princess Chichibu|1=Setsuko, Princess Chichibu}} (née {{ill|Matsudaira clan|en|Matsudaira clan|qid=Q1141077|lt=Matsudaira|1=Matsudaira clan}}).<gallery mode="packed"> File:Seiyokan (Nabeshima residence in Tokyo).jpg|Tokyo house of Marquess {{ill|Nabeshima Naohiro (Saga)|en|Nabeshima Naohiro (Saga)|qid=Q5357768|lt=Naohiro Nabeshima|1=Nabeshima Naohiro (Saga)}} File:Hofu Mouri Residence and Museum.JPG|Country house of Viscount [[Mototoshi Mori]] (now {{ill|Mōri Museum|en|Mōri Museum|qid=Q11547697|lt=Mori Museum|1=Mōri Museum}}) File:Former Maeda Estate 2009.jpg|Former residence of Marquess {{ill|Toshinari Maeda|en|Toshinari Maeda|qid=Q3532631|lt=Toshinari Maeda|1=Toshinari Maeda}} (now {{ill|Komaba Park|en|Komaba Park|qid=Q11668323|lt=Komaba Park|1=Komaba Park}}) File:View of Murin-an garden from main house.jpg|Former Kyoto House of Prince {{ill|Yamagata Aritomo|en|Yamagata Aritomo|qid=Q297636|lt=Aritomo Yamagata|1=Yamagata Aritomo}} File:Kazoku-Jogakko.JPG|Kazoku Girls' School ({{ill|Gakushūin|en|Gakushūin|qid=Q1061900|lt=Gakushuin|1=Gakushūin}} Girls' School) in 1889 File:Kaimei kizokuhyō by Shinsai.jpg|alt=Woodblock print by [[Kobayashi Toshimitsu]], "Table of Enlightened Aristocrats", 1877.
